source: Original KaiSip study notes, organized by The IIA's CIA Part 1 syllabus effective 2025. KaiSip is an independent study aid, not affiliated with or endorsed by The IIA.
overview: Section D is about fraud: what it is, why people commit it, where it is likely, which controls prevent or detect it, and what an internal auditor does on meeting a sign of it. The Global Internal Audit Standards say little about fraud, but say it firmly: consider fraud risk in every engagement risk assessment, weigh it as part of due professional care, and report concerns through the proper channel. Management owns fraud prevention, and an investigation needs the right mandate and skills.
analogy: Think of a lifeguard at a public pool. The lifeguard does not own the pool, mend the fence or write the rules; the pool manager does. But on every shift the lifeguard scans the water, knowing where swimmers get into trouble: the deep end, the crowded slide, the corner nobody watches. On seeing a sign of trouble, the lifeguard does not wait for the end-of-day report or start a private inquiry, but raises the alarm through the agreed signal. A rescue diver handles what needs diving skills. Internal auditors treat fraud risk in the same way.

topics.topic_name: Fraud triangle, fraud risks and schemes
topics.overview: Fraud is deliberate deception for a gain the person or organization has no right to. This topic explains what sets fraud apart from error, the three sides of the fraud triangle, how to recognize where fraud could happen, and the main families of fraud schemes.
can_do: Explain what separates fraud from an honest error
Describe each side of the fraud triangle and give an example of it
Recognize the conditions that make fraud more likely in a process
Match a described scheme to its family: false reporting, theft of assets or corruption

subtopics.name: Fraud and How It Differs from Error
subtopics.definition: Fraud is a deliberate act of deception, concealment or breach of trust by a person or organization to gain an advantage it is not entitled to.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Intent changes the response. An error needs a process fix; a suspected fraud needs careful reporting, protected evidence and often specialists.
how_it_works: Intent is the dividing line: an error is an honest mistake, while fraud is done on purpose and is usually hidden.
The gain can be money, property, a bonus or a business advantage; staff, managers, executives, suppliers, customers or outsiders can all commit it.
Clues that point toward intent: a pattern instead of a single slip, effort to hide the item, and reluctance to correct it once raised.
Small amounts still count: practitioners quoted in The IIA's 2026 white paper on fraud risk warn that frauds tend to start small and grow.
An internal auditor reports what the evidence shows and that it may indicate fraud. Deciding that fraud happened is for an investigation by qualified people.
subtopics.example: At a furniture exporter in Vietnam, internal auditor Linh finds a supplier paid twice: one mis-keyed invoice, refunded as soon as it was noticed. That is an error. Elsewhere, the same clerk split five invoices to stay under the approval limit, altered their dates and delayed answering questions. Linh records the pattern and the concealment as possible fraud indicators and takes them to the engagement supervisor.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Fraud needs intent; error does not. On CIA questions, the internal auditor judges intent from pattern and concealment, reports the indicators through the proper channel, and leaves the verdict to an investigation.

exam_traps.trap: The amount is too small to be fraud.
exam_traps.why: Size is not the test. A deliberate, concealed act for gain is fraud at any amount, and small frauds often grow.

exam_traps.trap: Any misstatement found in testing should be reported as fraud.
exam_traps.why: Without signs of intent it may be an honest mistake. Look for a pattern, concealment or resistance to correction first.

key_terms.definition: A deliberate act using deception or a breach of trust to gain something the person or organization has no right to.
The deliberate purpose behind an act; the feature that separates fraud from error.
Steps taken to hide an act, such as altered documents, false entries or withheld answers.

subtopics.name: The Fraud Triangle
subtopics.definition: The fraud triangle is a model of three conditions that accompany a fraud: motivation, opportunity and rationalization.
subtopics.why_it_matters: The triangle turns a vague worry into three questions for any process: who is under pressure, where could they act unseen, and how would they excuse it?
how_it_works: Motivation is the incentive or pressure to act: personal debt, a bonus tied to targets, or fear of missing a sales or profit goal.
Opportunity is a gap that lets the act happen and stay hidden: one person controlling a whole transaction, shared passwords, or unreviewed payments.
Rationalization is the excuse that makes the act feel acceptable: 'they treat me unfairly', 'the company can afford it'.
The syllabus says motivation; The IIA's 2026 white paper says incentive or pressure. It is the same side.
Controls act mainly on opportunity, the side the white paper says internal auditors can most directly affect. Pressure and rationalization sit in people and culture.
One side alone proves nothing: hard targets are a reason to look closer at controls, not evidence of fraud.
subtopics.example: Internal auditor Tariq is planning a review of a regional sales office of a Jordanian telecom company. The quarterly bonus pays only above 110% of target (motivation), the sales manager can both create customer accounts and approve credits (opportunity), and staff say head office 'sets impossible numbers' (rationalization). Tariq adds account creation and credit approvals to the risks to test.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Know all three sides and which one controls reach. On CIA questions, segregation of duties, approvals and reviews reduce opportunity; pressure and rationalization are read from targets, rewards, culture and tone at the top.

exam_traps.trap: Strong process controls remove all three sides of the triangle.
exam_traps.why: Controls mostly close opportunity. A pressured person with an excuse may still collude or override, so culture and oversight matter too.

exam_traps.trap: A department under heavy target pressure must be committing fraud.
exam_traps.why: One side of the triangle is a risk indicator, not proof. It directs the auditor to the related controls.

key_terms.definition: The incentive or pressure that pushes a person toward fraud, such as debt or a target-based bonus.
A weakness that lets a person commit fraud and expect not to be caught.
The personal excuse a person uses to make a dishonest act feel justified.

subtopics.memory_aid: Why would they, how could they, and how would they excuse it?

subtopics.name: Recognizing Where Fraud Could Happen
subtopics.definition: A fraud risk is the possibility that someone will deliberately deceive in order to take assets, misstate information or gain an improper advantage in an activity.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Fraud risk is pervasive: it can sit in any process, at any level. An auditor who knows the usual conditions spots exposure early, before tests are designed around honest mistakes only.
how_it_works: Ask of each activity how someone could deliberately misstate, steal or conceal, and who would be motivated and able to do it.
Look for value that is easy to move: cash, payments, payroll, stock, refunds, and information such as customer data.
Look for open doors: one person handling a whole transaction, wide system access, shared passwords, or no independent review.
Look for pressure: bonuses tied to results, ambitious targets, or a culture where bad news is not tolerated.
Consider outsiders as well: suppliers, customers and cyber criminals, sometimes working with an insider.
A clean past does not lower the risk: fraud is hidden by design, so 'never had fraud here' is a belief, not evidence.
subtopics.example: During a walkthrough at a hospital pharmacy in Kenya, internal auditor Wanjiru learns that one technician orders stock, receives deliveries and adjusts the inventory system, and that high-value drugs are counted only once a year. Nobody has reported a loss. Wanjiru records theft of stock hidden by system adjustments as a fraud risk in the engagement risk assessment.

review: Walk one transaction from start to finish and note who touches it
Compare system access rights with each person's assigned duties
Trace bonus and target rules to the figures staff can influence
evidence: System access listing matched to job roles
Process map showing who initiates, approves and records
Bonus plan and target documents for the unit
audit_focus.recommend: Have process management separate conflicting duties or add an independent review where one person controls a transaction.
audit_focus.decides: Management of the activity decides how to treat each fraud risk

subtopics.isaca_rule: Fraud risk is a possibility, not a finding. On CIA questions, the internal auditor recognizes it from conditions (value, access, pressure, weak review) and does not wait for a past case or a tip.

exam_traps.trap: No fraud has been found here before, so the fraud risk is low.
exam_traps.why: Fraud is concealed, so an absence of known cases says little. Exposure is judged from conditions and controls.

exam_traps.trap: Fraud risk matters only in finance and accounting processes.
exam_traps.why: Fraud can involve operations, procurement, payroll, data and nonfinancial reports. Any activity with value and opportunity is exposed.

key_terms.definition: The chance that deliberate deception will harm an objective of the activity or the organization.
A risk that can arise in many processes and units at once; the Standards give fraud as an example.
Fraud committed against the organization by outside parties, such as suppliers, customers or cyber criminals.

subtopics.name: Common Fraud Schemes
subtopics.definition: A fraud scheme is the specific method used to commit and hide a fraud; most schemes fall into false reporting, theft of assets or corruption.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Naming the scheme tells the auditor which records to distrust and which control should have stopped it. A vague fear of fraud cannot be tested; a named scheme can.
how_it_works: Fraudulent reporting misstates information on purpose: sales invented or recorded early to meet a target, or uncollectible debts hidden with journal entries.
Asset misappropriation takes or misuses resources: inflated hours, payroll diverted to a private account, payment for goods never delivered, stock taken.
Corruption is misuse of position for an improper benefit, such as a bribe from a supplier, often alongside an undisclosed personal interest.
A scheme has two parts, the act and the cover. Forged signatures, altered documents and false entries are common cover.
Collusion, where two or more people act together, lets a scheme pass controls that depend on people checking each other.
The four families below follow the Fraud Risk Management Guide of COSO and the ACFE, two professional bodies; schemes range from a forged check to cyber fraud.

types.meaning: Deliberate misstatement of financial results or disclosures.
Deliberate misstatement of other reported information, such as safety, quality or sustainability figures.
Theft or misuse of cash, goods, equipment or information.
Misuse of position for an improper benefit, including bribery and other illegal acts.

subtopics.example: A grain cooperative in Argentina pays a transport contractor. Internal auditor Mateo notes three facts: invoices for trips the weighbridge never recorded, approval by a logistics supervisor who is the contractor's cousin, and round amounts paid within a day. Mateo classes the risk as asset misappropriation through false billing, with possible corruption, and plans tests matching invoices to weighbridge records.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Classify a scheme by what is abused: information (fraudulent reporting), resources (asset misappropriation) or position (corruption). On CIA questions, the family points to the control that failed and the records to test.

exam_traps.trap: Fraud always means stealing cash or goods.
exam_traps.why: Misstating results to earn a bonus or hide a loss is fraud too, even when nothing leaves a safe or a warehouse.

exam_traps.trap: A bribe paid to win business is not fraud, because the organization benefits.
exam_traps.why: The Standards' definition covers an unjust or illegal business advantage as well as personal gain. Corruption is a fraud family.

key_terms.definition: The method by which a fraud is carried out and hidden.
Two or more people working together to get around a control.
Offering or taking something of value to influence a decision improperly.

topics.topic_name: Weighing fraud risk in an engagement
topics.overview: Every engagement risk assessment must consider fraud. This topic covers that requirement, how auditors think through fraud scenarios while planning, and how to judge which processes are exposed enough to change the engagement's objectives, scope, tests or team.
can_do: Decide when fraud risk must be considered in an engagement and what differs for advisory work
Judge from planning facts which fraud scenarios deserve testing
Determine which process in a scenario carries the greatest fraud exposure, and why
Decide what to adjust (objectives, scope, tests, skills) when fraud risk is significant

subtopics.name: Fraud in the Engagement Risk Assessment
subtopics.definition: The engagement risk assessment is the planning step in which internal auditors identify and rank the risks of the activity under review, fraud risks included.
subtopics.why_it_matters: This is where the Standards speak most directly about fraud. An engagement planned without asking how fraud could occur tests only for honest mistakes.
how_it_works: Standard 13.2 Engagement Risk Assessment: internal auditors must consider fraud-related risks when identifying the risks to review, in every engagement and not only in fraud audits.
Standard 4.2 Due Professional Care: care includes weighing how probable significant errors, fraud and noncompliance are.
It happens in planning, before objectives, scope and the work program are settled, so that fraud risks can shape them.
Fraud risks are ranked like other risks, by likelihood and impact, and the most significant go into the work program.
In an advisory engagement, the agreement with stakeholders may make a formal, written risk assessment unnecessary.
If an earlier engagement assessed the same activity, the auditors review and update that assessment, fraud risks included.
subtopics.example: Internal auditor Ayasha is planning an assurance engagement on grant payments at a Canadian arts council. The grants manager says a fraud review is unnecessary because the external auditors found nothing. Ayasha still lists fraud risks (false applicants, staff approving grants to relatives), rates them, and agrees with the engagement supervisor which ones the work program will cover.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Fraud risk is considered in every engagement risk assessment, during planning. On CIA questions, 'only when management asks', 'only in a fraud audit' and 'after fieldwork' are wrong; the advisory exception is about a formal, documented assessment.

exam_traps.trap: Fraud risk is assessed only in a fraud audit or when management asks.
exam_traps.why: Standard 13.2 makes it part of identifying risks in each engagement. Neither the label nor a request switches it on.

exam_traps.trap: An advisory engagement always needs a formal, documented fraud risk assessment.
exam_traps.why: For advisory work, the agreement with stakeholders decides whether a formal, documented assessment is needed.

key_terms.definition: The planning work that identifies the activity's significant risks, fraud included, and ranks them for review.
The care and skill a prudent, competent internal auditor applies, including weighing the chance of significant fraud.
The planned list of tasks and tests that will meet the engagement objectives.

subtopics.name: Fraud Brainstorming and Scenario Thinking
subtopics.definition: Fraud brainstorming is a planning discussion in which the engagement team imagines how fraud could be committed and hidden in the activity.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Fraud is designed to pass ordinary checks. Thinking like someone who wants to beat the process shows which controls matter and where a routine sample would see nothing.
how_it_works: Gather information first: process documents, walkthroughs, interviews, earlier results, and risk assessments done by management or others.
Brainstorm scenarios: who could misstate, steal or conceal, with what access, under what pressure, and how it would be hidden.
Rate each fraud risk for significance, then decide which ones the engagement will examine further and with which tests.
Involve different levels and, where sensible, the business. Ask how a control could be done differently; owners rarely suspect their own area.
Treat management's fraud risk assessment as input: the Standards advise relying on it only after concluding that the risk management processes are effective (a 'should').
Data analysis can show what interviews miss: outliers, overrides, policy exceptions and unseparated duties.
subtopics.example: Planning a procurement engagement at a Polish city transport operator, internal auditors Zofia and Emeka brainstorm with a buyer and a warehouse lead. Asked how the three-quote rule could be done differently, the buyer says quotes arrive by personal email. The team writes a scenario (one supplier sending all three quotes), rates it high, and adds a test of quote sources to the work program.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Imagine the scheme before choosing the tests. On CIA questions, the internal auditor brainstorms fraud scenarios during planning, challenges management's assessment, and carries significant scenarios into the work program.

exam_traps.trap: Management has already assessed fraud risk, so the auditor can adopt its ratings.
exam_traps.why: Management's view is input. The auditor applies skepticism and should rely on it only once the risk management processes are judged effective.

exam_traps.trap: Brainstorming is best left until testing turns up something odd.
exam_traps.why: Its purpose is to shape objectives, scope and tests. After fieldwork it can no longer direct the work.

key_terms.definition: A team discussion during planning about how fraud could occur and be concealed in the activity.
Following a transaction step by step to see how the process really works and where the controls sit.
Examining whole sets of records with software to find patterns, outliers and exceptions.

subtopics.name: Processes with High Fraud Exposure
subtopics.definition: Fraud exposure is how open a process is to fraud, judged from what is at stake, who has access, the pressure on people and the strength of controls.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Engagement time is limited. Judging exposure tells the auditor which processes need deeper tests, more experienced staff or specialist help, and which need only standard coverage.
how_it_works: High stakes: the process moves money or valuable assets, or produces figures that drive bonuses, funding or outside confidence.
Easy access: a few people control the whole transaction, or system rights are wider than jobs need.
Strong pressure: demanding targets, rewards that depend on one number, or results that are always good.
Weak oversight: skipped or routine reviews, reconciliations with old open items, and many overrides or exceptions.
The IIA's 2026 white paper points to payments, payroll, and sales or trading teams working under profit targets.
When exposure is significant, objectives, scope, tests and team skills are adjusted. Resource or skill gaps must be raised with the chief audit executive (Standard 13.5 Engagement Resources).
subtopics.example: At a microfinance lender in Bangladesh, internal auditor Farhana compares two processes. Staff training has a small budget and three approvers. Loan disbursement moves cash daily, branch officers both approve and release loans, and branches are ranked on monthly volume. Farhana rates disbursement as the high-exposure process, widens its scope, and asks the engagement supervisor for an auditor skilled in data analysis.

review: Compare each process step with who can initiate, approve, record and hold assets
Trace targets and ranking rules to the figures staff control
Sample overrides and policy exceptions for approval and stated reason
evidence: Data extract of overrides, exceptions and manual adjustments
User access report for the process systems
Target, ranking and incentive documents
audit_focus.recommend: Have process management strengthen review and separate duties in the steps that carry the highest fraud exposure.
audit_focus.decides: Management of the activity decides the control response and owns the risk

subtopics.isaca_rule: Exposure follows value, access, pressure and weak oversight, not the size of the department or its clean record. On CIA questions, significant fraud exposure changes the engagement's scope, tests and staffing.

exam_traps.trap: The process with the largest budget always has the highest fraud risk.
exam_traps.why: Size is one factor. A smaller process with cash, one person in control and target pressure can be far more exposed.

exam_traps.trap: If the team lacks fraud-testing skills, the fraud risk can be left out of scope without comment.
exam_traps.why: Skill gaps go to the chief audit executive, who can obtain the competencies. Silently dropping a significant risk hides a limit on the work.

key_terms.definition: The degree to which a process is open to fraud, given its value, access, pressure and controls.
A transaction allowed outside the normal rule; each one needs a reason and an approval.

topics.topic_name: Fraud risk management and red flags
topics.overview: Organizations manage fraud risk through governance, risk assessment, controls, reporting channels, investigation and monitoring. This topic covers how an internal auditor evaluates that program, how to notice and weigh red flags across the organization and inside a process, and what to do with a red flag found during an engagement.
can_do: Judge whether an organization's fraud program has the parts a sound one needs
Weigh red flags in a scenario and decide whether they call for more work or escalation
Decide to whom, when and how a red flag found during an engagement is reported
Distinguish reporting an indicator from accusing a person or concluding that fraud occurred

subtopics.name: Evaluating Fraud Risk Management
subtopics.definition: Fraud risk management is the organization's set of policies, assessments, controls, reporting channels and responses for preventing, detecting and dealing with fraud.
subtopics.why_it_matters: The board and senior management are responsible for managing fraud risk. Internal audit gives assurance on whether their program is well designed and working, and advises on gaps.
how_it_works: Roles: senior management designs and runs the program and sets the tone, the board oversees it, and internal audit assesses it.
A widely used guide from COSO and the ACFE, two professional bodies, describes five parts: governance, risk assessment, preventive and detective controls, reporting and investigation, and monitoring.
For each part, ask whether it is adequately designed and whether it operates effectively.
A sound fraud risk assessment names schemes, rates how likely and serious each is, maps existing controls, and acts on what remains.
The IIA's position paper on fraud adds a fraud response plan saying who does what when fraud is suspected, internal audit included.
The internal audit plan must consider coverage of fraud risk (Standard 9.4 Internal Audit Plan).
subtopics.example: Internal auditor Babajide reviews fraud risk management at a Norwegian ferry operator. There is an anti-fraud policy and a hotline, but the last fraud risk assessment is four years old, lists no schemes and has no owner, and nobody knows who would investigate a tip. Babajide reports the program as incompletely designed and recommends that management assign ownership and refresh the assessment.

review: Compare the program with the five parts of a sound fraud risk program
Inspect the latest fraud risk assessment for schemes, ratings and owners
Trace two reported concerns from receipt to resolution
evidence: Case log showing intake, investigation and outcome dates
Latest fraud risk assessment document with its approval date
Board or committee minutes covering fraud reporting
audit_focus.recommend: Have senior management assign an owner, update the fraud risk assessment and define who investigates reported concerns.
audit_focus.decides: Senior management decides how to close gaps in the program

subtopics.isaca_rule: Management owns fraud risk management, the board oversees it, and internal audit evaluates and advises. On CIA questions, internal audit running the anti-fraud program or guaranteeing prevention is the wrong answer.

exam_traps.trap: Internal audit is responsible for preventing and detecting fraud.
exam_traps.why: Management is. Internal audit gives assurance over the controls and the program and advises, without taking on management's responsibility.

exam_traps.trap: An anti-fraud policy and a hotline show that fraud risk management is effective.
exam_traps.why: Those are two pieces of design. Effectiveness also needs a current risk assessment, working controls, a tested response and monitoring.

key_terms.definition: A structured review that identifies possible fraud schemes, rates them and maps the controls against them.
Written policies and investigation methods setting out who does what when fraud is suspected.
Discouraging fraud by making it likely that anyone who tries will be caught and punished.

subtopics.name: Red Flags Across the Organization and in a Process
subtopics.definition: A red flag is a fact, pattern or behavior suggesting that fraud may be present and deserves a closer look; it is an indicator, not proof.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Most frauds are hidden, so auditors meet them first as small oddities. Weighing them calmly avoids both blindness and false accusation.
how_it_works: Organization-wide: heavy target pressure, leaders who set controls aside or discourage questions, a belief that fraud cannot happen here, and shared passwords.
In a process: many corrections or reversals, reconciling items (unexplained differences) left open or undated, missing documents, results that are always good, and slow answers to audit requests.

Behavioral flags found in fraud examiners' surveys, cited in The IIA's 2026 white paper: living beyond one's means, money troubles, unusual closeness to a supplier, refusing to share duties, defensiveness.
Weigh a flag before acting: is there an innocent explanation, does independent evidence support it, is it a pattern, and what could be lost?
Standard 4.3 Professional Skepticism requires seeking more evidence when information looks incomplete, inconsistent, false or misleading. It does not mean assuming dishonesty.
subtopics.example: Reviewing a supplier ledger reconciliation at a Chilean winery, internal auditor Renata sees six undated reconciling items carried for three years, and the accountant has ignored three requests for support. Each fact alone might be sloppiness; together they form a pattern. Renata widens the sample, obtains bank records directly, documents the facts and briefs the engagement supervisor the same day.

review: Compare the flagged item with independent records obtained directly
Sample similar transactions to see whether the oddity repeats
Trace who created, approved and changed the flagged entries
evidence: System audit trail of who posted and changed entries
Bank or third-party records obtained directly
Aged list of unresolved differences with supporting papers
audit_focus.recommend: Have senior management arrange an investigation by qualified people when indicators remain unexplained after follow-up.
audit_focus.decides: Senior management or the board, under the fraud response plan, decides whether to investigate

subtopics.isaca_rule: A red flag starts work; it does not end it. On CIA questions, the internal auditor corroborates with independent evidence, looks for a pattern, and escalates the indicators without treating one flag as proof.

exam_traps.trap: One red flag, such as an employee's expensive car, is enough to conclude that fraud occurred.
exam_traps.why: A single flag can have an innocent cause. It justifies more evidence and escalation of facts, never a conclusion about a person.

exam_traps.trap: A reasonable explanation from the manager closes the matter.
exam_traps.why: Skepticism means corroborating statements with evidence from an independent source, especially when the person explaining could be involved.

key_terms.definition: A warning sign that fraud may exist; a reason to look closer, not proof.
An attitude of testing whether information can be trusted before relying on it, without assuming dishonesty.
Checking a statement or record against a second, independent source.

subtopics.name: Reporting Red Flags Found During an Engagement
subtopics.definition: Reporting a red flag means passing documented facts that may indicate fraud, promptly, to people with authority to act, through the channels policy and law set.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Handled badly, a red flag can alert a wrongdoer, destroy evidence, harm an innocent person or let losses continue.
how_it_works: Document the facts and raise them promptly with the engagement supervisor or chief audit executive, following the function's methodology (a 'should' under Standard 1.2).
Do not wait for the final communication: matters needing immediate attention are raised during the engagement (a consideration to Standard 13.1 Engagement Communication).
Unethical conduct must be reported under organizational policies (Standard 1.2); so must legal or regulatory violations, to those with authority to act (Standard 1.3 Legal and Ethical Behavior).
Bypass anyone who may be involved. If senior management is implicated, the chief audit executive should report to the board.
Report indicators, not verdicts: what was found and why it may indicate fraud. Do not confront or accuse.
Never drop or soften the matter: Standard 1.1 Honesty and Professional Courage forbids hiding or leaving out findings.
subtopics.example: While testing travel claims at a Malaysian engineering firm, internal auditor Hafiz finds that the finance manager, the engagement's main contact, approved eleven of their own claims using altered hotel receipts. Hafiz secures copies, tells no one in finance, and briefs the chief audit executive that afternoon. Under the fraud response policy, the chief audit executive takes the matter to the audit committee chair.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Facts, promptly, to the right level, through the set channel. On CIA questions, the internal auditor usually escalates inside internal audit first, bypasses anyone possibly involved, and does not confront the suspect.

exam_traps.trap: Discuss the red flag with the manager of the activity first, like any other finding.
exam_traps.why: That manager may be involved or may alert whoever is. Suspected fraud goes up through internal audit to those with authority to act.

exam_traps.trap: Go straight to the police or a regulator.
exam_traps.why: Outside reporting follows what laws, regulations and policies specify. Acting alone may breach confidentiality duties and harm a later investigation.

key_terms.definition: Passing a matter up to a higher level of authority that can act on it.
The route that policy or law sets for raising a concern, such as a supervisor, ethics office or board.

topics.topic_name: Controls that prevent and detect fraud
topics.overview: Fraud controls either stop a fraud before it happens (preventive) or reveal it soon afterward (detective). This topic explains tone at the top, segregation of duties and authority levels, and the detective controls the syllabus names: reconciliations, supervisory reviews and whistleblower hotlines. No control gives absolute assurance, because collusion and management override can defeat it.
can_do: Explain how tone at the top raises or lowers the chance of fraud
Describe which duties are kept apart and what management can do when they cannot be
Explain how approval limits prevent fraud and how people get around them
Tell preventive from detective fraud controls in a short scenario

subtopics.name: Tone at the Top and the Likelihood of Fraud
subtopics.definition: Tone at the top is the message about integrity that the board and senior management send through what they say, do, reward and tolerate.
subtopics.why_it_matters: People copy what leaders reward. Leaders who bend rules hand staff a ready excuse and weaken every other control.
how_it_works: Senior management sets the tone that shapes the whole culture; the board sets integrity expectations and oversees how management lives up to them.
Tone works on the human sides of the fraud triangle: it weakens rationalization and, through realistic targets and fair rewards, eases undue pressure.
It shows in actions more than documents: how leaders react to bad news, and whether rule-breakers who deliver results are disciplined.
The board is a check on management override and deals with allegations about senior management.
A code of conduct shows intent only; the tone is real when the code is followed at the top and enforced the same way for everyone.
Internal auditors must encourage an ethics-based culture and report conduct that breaks the organization's ethical expectations (Standard 1.2 Organization's Ethical Expectations).
subtopics.example: A Ghanaian mobile money company has a clear code of conduct. Internal auditor Akosua learns that the top-selling regional head was caught backdating agent contracts and received only a private warning, then the annual sales award. Staff now describe backdating as tolerated. Akosua reports that the enforced tone contradicts the written one and raises the likelihood of fraud across sales.

review: Compare disciplinary outcomes for senior and junior staff after similar breaches
Sample ethics survey and hotline data for themes about leaders
Trace incentive plans to the pressure they put on reported results
evidence: Disciplinary case records by grade and outcome
Staff ethics survey results and hotline statistics
Code of conduct sign-offs and training completion records
audit_focus.recommend: Have senior management apply the same consequences to everyone and review incentives that reward results at any cost.
audit_focus.decides: The board holds senior management to account for its conduct

subtopics.isaca_rule: Judge tone by what leaders do and enforce, not by what the policy says. On CIA questions, a weak tone at the top raises the likelihood of fraud even where process controls look strong.

exam_traps.trap: A signed code of conduct proves a strong tone at the top.
exam_traps.why: A document shows intent. Tone is what leaders model, reward and punish; an unenforced code can signal that rules are for show.

exam_traps.trap: Good process controls make tone at the top irrelevant to fraud.
exam_traps.why: Controls can be overridden by management or beaten by collusion. Culture decides whether people try, and whether others speak up.

key_terms.definition: The example and expectations about integrity set by the board and senior management.
Managers using their authority to set aside controls that bind everyone else.
Shared values and habits that make honest behavior the normal, expected choice.

subtopics.name: Segregation of Duties
subtopics.definition: Segregation of duties is the practice of dividing a transaction's key steps among different people so that no one person can both commit and hide a fraud.
subtopics.why_it_matters: It is the main control against opportunity. If one person can start, approve and record a transaction and hold the asset, nothing independent checks it.
how_it_works: Key steps to keep apart: initiating a transaction, approving it, recording it, handling the money or goods, and reconciling the records.
It applies inside systems too: the person who creates a supplier should not be able to approve its payments.
It works before the event, which is why it counts as a preventive control.
Shared passwords, staff covering for each other, and one manager holding several system roles quietly cancel the separation.
Collusion defeats it: two people acting together can pass a control that depends on their independence.
Where full separation is not practical, as in a small team, management chooses alternative controls such as closer supervisory review.
subtopics.example: At the three-person finance office of a New Zealand honey exporter, internal auditor Mere finds that the accountant sets up suppliers, enters invoices and releases bank payments. Hiring more staff is impossible. Mere recommends that management move payment release to the owner and have the owner review a monthly report of new suppliers and changed bank details.

review: Compare system access rights with a matrix of conflicting duties
Sample transactions and confirm different people initiated and approved them
Inspect how alternative controls operate where duties are combined
evidence: System-generated user access report with roles
Transaction logs showing initiator and approver identities
Records of supervisory review where duties are combined
audit_focus.recommend: Have process management remove conflicting access rights or add an independent review where duties cannot be separated.
audit_focus.decides: Management of the activity treats or accepts any remaining conflict

subtopics.isaca_rule: No one person should control a transaction from start to finish. On CIA questions, test whether the separation is real in system access; where it cannot be achieved, expect alternative controls chosen by management.

exam_traps.trap: Duties are separated on the organization chart, so the control is working.
exam_traps.why: Shared logins, wide system access or colleagues covering for each other can undo it. The test is who can actually do what.

exam_traps.trap: A small team that cannot separate duties has no acceptable control option.
exam_traps.why: Management can choose alternative controls, such as an owner's or supervisor's review of that person's work.

key_terms.definition: Dividing a transaction's key steps among different people so no one can commit and hide a fraud alone.
Tasks that, held by one person, would let that person both make and hide an error or fraud.
A different control that management uses when the preferred one, such as separating duties, is not practical.

subtopics.name: Authority Levels and Approval Limits
subtopics.definition: Authority levels are documented limits on who may approve which transactions and up to what amount, with larger or riskier items needing a more senior approver.
subtopics.why_it_matters: An approval limit puts a second, accountable person in front of a transaction before it happens, shrinking one person's opportunity to commit the organization improperly.
how_it_works: A delegation of authority sets limits by role: a supervisor approves up to one amount, a director up to a higher one, the board above that.
The control is preventive: the transaction should not go ahead until someone with enough authority, independent of the requester, has approved it.
Limits are strongest when the system enforces them, refusing approvals above a user's limit or by the requester.
Ways around a limit: splitting one purchase into several smaller ones, approving one's own request, or a senior manager overriding the rule.
An approver who signs without reading the support adds no control: approving means checking that the transaction is valid, supported and within policy.
subtopics.example: A Dubai hotel group requires a director's approval for purchases above 20,000 dirhams. Internal auditor Samira analyzes purchase data and finds 14 orders to one decorator, each between 19,500 and 19,900 dirhams, within two months, all approved by the same purchasing supervisor. Samira documents the pattern as possible splitting and takes it to the engagement supervisor as a fraud indicator.

review: Compare approvals in a transaction sample with the delegation of authority
Sample purchases just below limits by supplier and period
Reperform an approval attempt beyond a test user's limit
evidence: Data analysis of transactions clustered just under approval thresholds
Screenshot of the thresholds configured for each role
Current delegation of authority with its approval record
audit_focus.recommend: Have management enforce approval limits in the system and monitor purchases that cluster just below the limits.
audit_focus.decides: Senior management, within powers the board has set, decides who may approve what

subtopics.isaca_rule: Approval limits prevent fraud only when the approver is independent, has the authority and truly reviews. On CIA questions, authority levels are preventive controls, and many items just under a limit are a red flag.

exam_traps.trap: Authority limits are detective controls because they involve a review.
exam_traps.why: The approval comes before the transaction goes ahead, so it prevents. A check after the event, such as a reconciliation, detects.

exam_traps.trap: Every transaction was approved, so the authority control is effective.
exam_traps.why: Approvals by the requester, above the approver's limit, or of split purchases defeat it. Test who approved, when, and for how much.

key_terms.definition: The largest amount or the type of transaction that a role is allowed to approve.
Breaking one transaction into smaller ones so that each falls below an approval limit.
A control that stops an error or fraud before the transaction is completed.

subtopics.name: Detective Controls: Reconciliations, Supervisory Review and Hotlines
subtopics.definition: Detective fraud controls are checks that reveal a fraud or error after it has occurred, soon enough to limit the loss and trace what happened.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Prevention never works perfectly, because people collude and managers override. Detective controls shorten the time a fraud runs, and knowing that checks exist discourages people from trying.
how_it_works: A reconciliation compares two records that should agree, such as the ledger and the bank statement, and follows up every difference.
A supervisory review is a manager's examination of work, exceptions and reports, looking for items that are unusual, unsupported or outside policy.
A whistleblower hotline lets employees and others report concerns in confidence, often anonymously. Research cited in a widely used fraud risk guide finds most frauds are discovered through tips.
Each works only when done by someone independent of the work checked, on time, with differences and reports followed up to a conclusion.
The syllabus lists all three as controls that detect fraud; the same guide also credits reporting systems with preventing and deterring it.
The Standards name four control types in a consideration to Standard 13.2: preventive, detective, directive and corrective.

rows.label: What it does
cells: Matches two records and explains each difference
A manager examines work, exceptions and reports

rows.label: What it can reveal
cells: Missing cash, false entries, unrecorded items
Schemes hidden from the records, collusion, override

rows.label: What weakens it
cells: Prepared by the person who keeps the records; old items left open
Signing without reading; no follow-up of exceptions
Fear of retaliation; reports not investigated

subtopics.example: At a university bookshop in Trinidad, the cashier also prepares the daily till-to-bank reconciliation, and it always balances. An anonymous hotline call says refunds are being faked. Internal auditor Dwayne notes that the reconciler was not independent, passes the tip to the chief audit executive, and recommends that management assign the reconciliation to someone outside the bookshop.

review: Reperform a sample of reconciliations and trace old open items
Inspect review evidence for questions raised, not only signatures
Trace hotline reports from intake to documented outcome
evidence: Reperformed reconciliations compared with the originals
Hotline case log with dates, handling and outcomes
Review sign-offs with notes on exceptions followed up
audit_focus.recommend: Have management assign reconciliations and reviews to staff independent of the work and track open items to closure.
audit_focus.decides: Management owns the detective controls; the board oversees how reported concerns are handled

subtopics.isaca_rule: Reconciliations, supervisory reviews and hotlines detect; segregation of duties and approval limits prevent. On CIA questions, a detective control performed by the person whose work it checks, or never followed up, is not operating.

exam_traps.trap: A reconciliation prevents fraud because it is performed every month.
exam_traps.why: It happens after the transactions, so it detects. Its regularity may deter, but it does not stop the entry being made.

exam_traps.trap: The reconciliation is signed off, so it is effective.
exam_traps.why: A sign-off over old unexplained items, or one prepared by the person who records the transactions, gives little assurance.

key_terms.definition: A control that finds an error or fraud after it has happened.
Information about suspected wrongdoing given by an employee, supplier, customer or other person.
Punishing or disadvantaging a person for raising a concern in good faith.

topics.overview: Investigating fraud is specialist work. This topic covers the internal audit function's role, which depends on its mandate and its competencies, and then, at recognition level, how interviews, investigations and fraud tests are approached. It ends with how internal auditors work with fraud investigators and use what they know.
can_do: Explain what decides whether internal audit investigates a suspected fraud
Recognize sound and unsound interviewing practice in a short scenario
Recognize common investigation steps and fraud tests, and what each is for
Identify the information held by investigators that helps plan audit work

subtopics.name: The Internal Audit Function's Role in Investigations
subtopics.definition: The internal audit function's investigation role is whatever its mandate assigns and its competencies allow; investigating is not automatically part of internal auditing.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Investigations can end in dismissal, recovery action or prosecution. Without the authority or the skill, the work can spoil evidence and accuse the wrong person.
how_it_works: Mandate: the charter may define the function's services specifically, and the Standards give investigations as an example (a consideration to Standard 6.1 Internal Audit Mandate).
Competency: internal auditors must take on only services they have, or can obtain, the competencies for (Standard 3.1 Competency).
The chief audit executive must make sure the function as a whole has the competencies for its charter's services, or obtains them, for example from outside.
The IIA's position paper on fraud says investigating is not normally internal audit's job and is best done by people experienced in it.
Every internal auditor still needs enough fraud knowledge to spot red flags, judge whether to recommend an investigation, and evaluate anti-fraud controls.
After a fraud, internal audit's natural part is to learn how the controls failed and recommend improvements.
subtopics.example: A hotline report alleges theft of ticket revenue at a Peruvian rail operator, and the chief executive asks chief audit executive Rosa to have internal audit investigate. The charter lists investigations, but nobody on the team has investigation experience. Rosa tells the chief executive and the audit committee chair, and proposes that an outside forensic firm lead while internal audit supplies process knowledge.

review: Compare the charter's list of services with investigations actually performed
Inspect the fraud response plan for who leads each type of case
Evaluate investigators' qualifications against the cases assigned to them
evidence: Board-approved internal audit charter naming the services
Fraud response plan with roles and escalation routes
Skills records or contracts for the investigators used
audit_focus.recommend: Have senior management and the board define in the fraud response plan who investigates and when specialists are engaged.
audit_focus.decides: The board approves the charter that sets internal audit's investigation role

subtopics.isaca_rule: Two tests decide the role: is it in the mandate, and does the function have, or can it obtain, the competencies? On CIA questions, internal audit does not lead an investigation by default.

exam_traps.trap: Internal audit leads every fraud investigation because it is independent.
exam_traps.why: Independence is not investigative skill or authority. The role comes from the mandate, and the work needs people experienced in investigations.

exam_traps.trap: Internal auditors need no fraud knowledge when a separate investigations unit exists.
exam_traps.why: They must still consider fraud risk in every engagement, recognize red flags and evaluate anti-fraud controls.

key_terms.definition: A structured inquiry to establish the facts of a suspected fraud.
Specialist fact-finding on records and data, done so the results can support a dispute or legal case.
A specialist trained and experienced in investigating fraud.

subtopics.name: Interviewing Techniques
subtopics.definition: Interviewing is gathering information by asking people planned questions; in fraud-related work its aim is facts, never an accusation.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Interviews show how a process really runs and what people have seen. Handled badly, they warn a wrongdoer, pressure an innocent person or produce statements nobody can rely on.
how_it_works: Prepare: learn the process, read the documents, decide which facts are needed, and plan whom to see and what to ask.
Start with open questions that invite explanation ('Walk me through how a refund is approved'), then narrow to dates, amounts and names.
Ask how a control could be done differently or bypassed; people describe weaknesses more freely than fraud.
Stay neutral and respectful: Standard 1.1 requires truthful, respectful communication even when expressing skepticism. No threats, tricks or accusations.
Treat answers as information to corroborate against documents, data or an independent person, not as proof.
Record who attended and what was said. Questioning a suspected person is left to trained investigators.
subtopics.example: Internal auditor Sina is asked to gather background on petty cash shortages at a Samoan resort before investigators arrive. Sina asks the night clerk to describe the end-of-shift count, listens, and learns that the supervisor often counts alone. Sina does not ask who took the money, writes up the notes the same day and passes them to the chief audit executive.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Interview to learn facts, in an open, neutral and respectful way, and corroborate what is said. On CIA questions, an accusing style or an untrained auditor confronting the suspect is the wrong answer.

exam_traps.trap: A good fraud interview confronts the person early to get a confession.
exam_traps.why: Confrontation by an untrained auditor risks a wrongful accusation and damaged evidence. Suspect interviews belong to trained investigators.

exam_traps.trap: What a credible manager says in an interview can be taken as fact.
exam_traps.why: Skepticism requires corroboration. A statement is weaker than evidence the auditor obtains directly or from an independent source.

key_terms.definition: A question that asks for an explanation in the person's own words, not a yes or no.
A question answered with a specific fact, such as yes, no, a date or an amount.
A question worded so that it suggests the answer the interviewer wants.

subtopics.name: Investigation and Fraud Testing Techniques
subtopics.definition: Investigation techniques establish the facts of a suspected fraud; fraud tests are audit procedures that look for signs of deliberate manipulation in records.
subtopics.why_it_matters: At this level the task is recognition: what these methods are, what each is for, and why evidence must stay usable in discipline or court.
how_it_works: A sound investigation is prompt, competent and confidential, and follows a process planned in advance.
Typical steps: secure the evidence, examine documents and data, interview people, analyze the facts, report to those with authority, and fix the root cause.
Evidence, including digital evidence, must be collected lawfully and kept intact, respecting access rights and legal requirements.
Specialists join as needed: legal counsel, human resources, fraud examiners, digital forensic experts or outside investigators.
Fraud tests use data analysis over whole populations to find trends, outliers, manual overrides and unreported policy exceptions.
Other tests: tracing transactions to source documents, confirming facts with independent third parties, comparing related figures such as payroll cost and headcount, and widening a sample.
subtopics.example: After a tip about fake suppliers at a Hungarian printing company, the audit committee appoints an outside forensic firm. Internal auditor Bence supports it by comparing every supplier's bank account and address with the employee master file. Three matches appear. Bence does not question the employees, keeps the data extract unchanged with a note of how it was obtained, and hands the results to the investigators.

review: Sample closed cases and compare their handling with the fraud response plan
Inspect how evidence was secured and who had access to it
Evaluate whether root causes of confirmed cases were fixed
evidence: Case files with dated evidence logs and approvals
Records of legal advice on evidence collection
Corrective action tracking for confirmed cases
audit_focus.recommend: Have management document investigation procedures, including evidence handling and when legal counsel and specialists are engaged.
audit_focus.decides: Senior management, advised by legal counsel, decides on discipline, recovery and referral

subtopics.isaca_rule: Recognize each method and its purpose, and stay within your competence. On CIA questions, evidence is secured lawfully and kept intact, specialists lead, and data analysis over the full population is a typical fraud test.

exam_traps.trap: The auditor should copy the suspect's mailbox and files at once so no evidence is lost.
exam_traps.why: Collecting digital evidence without proper authority and method can break the law and make the evidence unusable.

exam_traps.trap: Fraud testing just means a larger random sample of the same documents.
exam_traps.why: Forged documents can pass a sample check. Fraud tests look for patterns across all the data and confirm facts independently.

key_terms.definition: Specialist collection and examination of electronic evidence so it stays reliable and lawful to use.
Keeping evidence unchanged and traceable from the moment it is obtained.
Asking an independent third party to verify a fact, such as a balance or a delivery.

subtopics.name: Working with Fraud Investigators
subtopics.definition: Coordination with fraud investigators is the sharing of plans, results and risk information between internal audit and those who investigate fraud, within confidentiality rules.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Investigators hold some of the best fraud risk information in the organization. Ignoring it leaves the audit blind to schemes already tried.
how_it_works: They hold useful information: their fraud risk assessments, files of past investigations, trends across cases, and whistleblower complaints.
In planning, the auditor may review recent risk assessments made by others and meet other assurance and advisory providers (Standard 13.2 considerations).
Trends point to exposure: several cases of one scheme, or complaints clustered on one unit, show where to test.
The chief audit executive is required to coordinate with other assurance providers, internal and external, and to consider relying on their work (Standard 9.5 Coordination and Reliance).
Confidentiality binds both sides: case details and whistleblower identities are shared only as policy and law allow (Standard 5.2 Protection of Information).
Stay clear of an open case: audit testing that touches it is agreed with the investigators first.
subtopics.example: Before an engagement on claims handling at a South African insurer, internal auditor Thabo meets the investigations unit lead. Its summary shows nine cases of claims paid to bank accounts changed days before payment, and five hotline complaints about one branch. Thabo adds bank-detail changes to the engagement risk assessment, brings that branch into scope, and agrees how case data will be handled.

review: Compare investigation trends with the fraud risks in the engagement risk assessment
Sample closed cases and trace whether the control fixes were made
Inspect how hotline complaints are logged, assigned and resolved
evidence: Investigation case statistics by scheme, unit and year
Hotline complaint log with handling status
Notes of coordination meetings between internal audit and investigators
audit_focus.recommend: Have management share investigation trends and case outcomes with process owners and track the resulting control fixes.
audit_focus.decides: Management decides on control fixes; investigators control access to open case files

subtopics.isaca_rule: Investigators' knowledge is planning input. On CIA questions, the internal auditor reviews their risk assessments, past cases, trends and complaints, respects confidentiality, and coordinates so an open investigation is not disturbed.

exam_traps.trap: Past investigation files are irrelevant once the cases are closed.
exam_traps.why: Closed cases show which schemes worked and which controls failed: direct evidence of exposure for the engagement risk assessment.

exam_traps.trap: Internal audit's access rights mean whistleblower identities can be shared freely within the team.
exam_traps.why: Access is for professional purposes only. Sensitive details go only to those who need them and are protected as policy and law require.

key_terms.definition: A person whose main job is to establish the facts of suspected fraud.
A pattern across cases, such as a repeated scheme, location or control weakness.
A concern about possible wrongdoing raised through a reporting channel, often in confidence.

key_terminologies.Fraud: A deliberate act using deception, hiding or a breach of trust to gain something the person or organization has no right to.
key_terminologies.Fraud triangle: A model of three conditions that accompany fraud: motivation, opportunity and rationalization.
key_terminologies.Motivation: The incentive or pressure that pushes a person toward fraud.
key_terminologies.Opportunity: A weakness that lets a person commit fraud and expect not to be caught.
key_terminologies.Rationalization: The excuse a person uses to make a dishonest act feel justified.
key_terminologies.Fraud risk: The chance that deliberate deception will harm an objective of an activity or the organization.
key_terminologies.Fraud scheme: The specific method by which a fraud is carried out and hidden.
key_terminologies.Fraudulent reporting: Deliberate misstatement of financial or nonfinancial information.
key_terminologies.Asset misappropriation: Theft or misuse of the organization's cash, goods, equipment or information.
key_terminologies.Corruption: Misuse of position for an improper benefit, such as taking a bribe.
key_terminologies.Collusion: Two or more people working together to get around a control.
key_terminologies.Management override: Managers using their authority to set aside controls that bind everyone else.
key_terminologies.Red flag: A warning sign that fraud may exist; a reason to look closer, not proof.
key_terminologies.Professional skepticism: An attitude of testing whether information can be trusted before relying on it, without assuming dishonesty.
key_terminologies.Engagement risk assessment: The planning step that identifies and ranks an activity's risks, fraud risks included.
key_terminologies.Fraud brainstorming: A planning discussion about how fraud could be committed and hidden in the activity under review.
key_terminologies.Fraud risk management: The policies, assessments, controls and responses an organization uses to prevent, detect and deal with fraud.
key_terminologies.Fraud response plan: Written policies and investigation methods setting out who does what when fraud is suspected.
key_terminologies.Tone at the top: The example and expectations about integrity set by the board and senior management.
key_terminologies.Segregation of duties: Dividing a transaction's key steps among different people so no one can commit and hide a fraud alone.
key_terminologies.Authority level: The largest amount or the type of transaction that a role may approve.
key_terminologies.Preventive control: A control that stops an error or fraud before the transaction is completed.
key_terminologies.Detective control: A control that finds an error or fraud after it has happened.
key_terminologies.Reconciliation: Comparing two records that should agree and following up every difference.
key_terminologies.Supervisory review: A manager's examination of work, exceptions and reports for unusual or unsupported items.
key_terminologies.Whistleblower hotline: A confidential channel for reporting suspected wrongdoing, often anonymously.
key_terminologies.Fraud investigation: A structured inquiry by qualified people to establish the facts of a suspected fraud.
key_terminologies.Forensic services: Specialist fact-finding work on records and data; the Standards list it as an example of advisory services.
key_terminologies.COSO: The Committee of Sponsoring Organizations, a private-sector body backed by five professional associations (The IIA is one) that publishes control, risk and fraud guidance.
key_terminologies.ACFE: The Association of Certified Fraud Examiners, a professional body for anti-fraud specialists.
